_about: A world, as one file. Fill it in, then run:
and when it reports clean, run it again without --dry-run.
Every block has a `_help` key explaining what it is and what it may contain.
`_help` keys are stripped on import; leave them or delete them, it makes no
`_layer` on each block says who owns it (see LAYERS.md):
world  — yours, nothing else has an opinion
kit    — you are replacing an engine default; fine, and only affects you
`_status` says how far the engine consumes it today:
live     — read by the engine now
stored   — saved on the record, not yet read by anything
planned  — has no home yet; the importer will tell you and skip it

_help: Identity. Becomes the `worlds` row. `genre` seeds your calendar and tone
set, so pick it before those blocks. `theme` is a one-word steer used in
scene prompts (grounded, cozy, light-novel...).
`image_profile` must be one the appliance supports; leave it unless you
know you want another.
world.name: Gaia
world.tagline: Seven nations. Seven magics. One world worth living in.
world.description: A world of seven great nations, each born from a different culture and each touched by a different kind of magic. Dragons, yokai, djinn, and spirits are part of daily life. The peace is fraying, the Old Roads are broken, and somewhere a soul new to this world is about to choose where to begin.

_help: How the world sounds. The engine already enforces how narration BEHAVES
— second person, player agency, who can know what. This is the part that
is yours: register, refusals, and whether there is a named narrator.
`narrator` empty means a clean unnamed narrator, which is a real choice.
A named one is a character, and characters can be wrong — say what they
are not allowed to know.
`sample_paragraph` is the most useful field here. Four sentences of an
ordinary moment in the voice you want.
voice.register: Warm, close, unhurried. Concrete nouns, plain verbs. The narrator notices small things — the smell of tea, light through a paper screen, the sound of a wooden bridge under weight. It does not rush. It lets a moment sit before moving on. It is fond of this world without being sentimental.
never: No prophecy. No one is chosen. The world does not have a destiny for anyone.
No mid-scene worldbuilding exposition. Characters do not explain how magic works unless asked.
No scene closes on weather alone. Close on something alive — a person acting, a decision landing, a door left open.
No narrative omniscience about what a character feels. Describe what is visible, not what is private.
No grimdark narration. The world can be cruel, but the narration is not cruel.
No fourth-wall breaks. The narrator never addresses the player.
voice.sample_paragraph: The road to Haru's shrine climbs through cedar shade, the air cool and smelling of moss even in summer. A fox watches from the stones near the second torii gate, not moving, its eyes the color of dark tea. Below, the town spreads out in rooftops of grey tile and garden green, smoke rising from the bathhouse chimney in a thin, patient line. Someone is practicing the shamisen, and the notes drift up the hill like they have nowhere else to be.

_help: What every picture in this world carries. `global_prompt` is appended to
each image prompt; `negative_prompt` is ruled out of all of them.
The engine decides SIZE and FRAMING per record type and you cannot change
those — a scene renders 1216x832, a record 896x1152, a portrait 832x1216,
because those are the image model's native buckets. See LAYERS.md.
`entry_type_styles` overrides the engine's per-type defaults. Leave it
empty and you inherit sensible ones. Overriding a style does NOT remove
the framing tags — you can restyle your art, you cannot make it
uncroppable.
art._layer: world, except entry_type_styles which is kit

_help: Time. Leave this block out entirely and you get a calendar seeded from
your genre, which is usually enough to start.
`day_phases` is what the tracker shows instead of clock time.
`start` is where the campaign opens; `month_index` is zero-based.

festivals.name: Moon-Viewing Night
festivals.description: On the fullest night of Mistveil the shrines hang paper lanterns over their ponds and the whole capital gathers on rooftops to watch the moon's reflection — the one night the kami of the moon is said to walk among the shrines. Rival clans share sake on the tea-house balconies; even the Ashikara and Takeda send quiet emissaries to sit at the same low table. The shrine keepers read the moon's reflection for the year's fortune, and a clear reflection is taken as a good omen for the truce between the houses.

festivals.name: Blossom-Viewing
festivals.description: When the cherry trees of the capital bloom in Blossom month, the tea schools carry their kettles into the orchards and brew beneath the falling petals for any who pass. Samurai lay down their swords for the afternoon, the Yokai walk openly in the lantern-lit groves, and a blossom that lands in a cup of tea is kept and pressed as a charm for the year. It is the gentlest day in Tsukuyomi, and the one most often cited by foreigners as the reason they love the shogunate.

festivals.name: Dragonfire Vow
festivals.description: At Highsun the Dragon Order gathers on the high meadow beneath Sunhelm Keep and re-enacts the old binding-vows before the silent wyrms in the peaks above. Knights kneel in full armor and speak the fire-oaths to a ridge where nothing answers but wind — and yet the rite is never skipped, because the day the Order stops speaking is the day they admit the bond is truly dead. The common folk picnic on the lower slopes, the Dawnfire priests bless the knights, and the elves of Elfshade watch from the treeline, saying nothing.

festivals.name: Harvestmoon Mead-Feast
festivals.description: When the highland hives are opened in Amberfall, the mead-brewers of Rivenspire tap the first casks and the realm drinks the year's honey-wine together. The noble houses lay tables in Crossford's market square beside the merchant guild's stalls, and the baronesses and the river-traders toast each other with the same cup. It is the closest thing Valdris has to a day without rank, and the Greyfen thieves, it is said, take the night off — even a syndicate needs a feast.

festivals.name: Lantern Night
festivals.description: In Frost month the people of all three states set paper lanterns on the river and let them float toward the sea, each lantern carrying the name of someone lost in the Last War. Jin, Chu, and Wei each light their own bank of the river, and the three streams of light merge where the waters bend — the one night the truce is felt rather than merely obeyed. The strategists of the Jade Pavilion walk the banks unarmed, and for that night no one schemes against anyone.

festivals.name: The Three-States Tea Conclave
festivals.description: Each Greenreach the tea houses of Chudu host the one gathering where envoys of Jin, Chu, and Wei will sit in the same room — the Three-States Tea Conclave, where the year's trade disputes are settled over cups before they become border disputes. The Five Schools of Tea pour in turn, each state's envoy chooses a cup without knowing whose school brewed it, and the ancient etiquette is that no one may draw a blade until the last cup is drunk. It is diplomacy performed as ceremony, and it has held the truce more than once.

festivals.name: Jaguar Moon
festivals.description: On the brightest night of Harvest the deep-canopy tribes gather at the Alta Canopy's great bough-hall and the jaguar-kin run the Moon Hunt — a ceremonial pursuit through the canopy to honor the jaguar-spirit pact, taking a single marked deer and no more. The shamans of the Still Water Lodge chant the old pact-words by firelight, and the Council of the Seven Boughs meets in full session for the only time each year, hearing disputes beneath the moon until dawn. A hunt that takes more than the one deer is taken as a warning that the pact is fraying.

festivals.name: The Serpent-Waking
festivals.description: In Deepwinter the guardians of the Coiled Serpent temple climb to the pyramid summit and perform the Waking rite over the sealed spirit-gate — not to wake the serpent, but to assure it is still sleeping. A single flute is played down the gate-shaft and the note that returns is listened to by the eldest guardian: a clear echo means the seal holds, a wavering echo means the shamans must be summoned. The river-traders bring offerings of fruit and fish to the plaza below, and no outsider is permitted above the stair's first landing.

festivals.name: Midwinter Blot
festivals.description: At the darkest turn of Deepwinter every longhouse in Hrafnland lights the midwinter fire and the jarls perform the Blot — the old sacrifice to the frost-giants and the wights, offering the first of the preserved meat and the first mead so the long winter will not take more. The völur of the Fog-Mother coven cast the runes at the Bone-Circle and read the coming year aloud to the jarls, who are supposed to heed them and often do not. It is the one night no raids are sailed and no feud is pursued; even Erik Stone-eye's young raiders sit by the fire and listen.

festivals.name: Longship Launch
festivals.description: When Frostwane breaks and the fjord ice loosens, the Longkeel Brotherhood slides the first new longship of the year down the Drekahöfn slipway and the High Jarl blesses its prow with mead from the ancestral horn. The raid crews gather to claim their berths, the rune-carvers cut the warding-runes into the new keel while the crowd watches, and the Thing of the Frost-Jarls votes the summer raiding targets on the same shore. It is the day Hrafnland turns its face outward again, and the day the southern coasts begin watching the sea.

festivals.name: Saffron Harvest
festivals.description: At Highsun the saffron crocus blooms across the oasis-valleys and the Saffron Houses of Zaffar lead the harvest at dawn, when each purple flower must be picked before the desert sun wilts it. The whole city rises before light, the binding families and the spice merchants work the same fields for one day, and the Grand Bazaar closes so that everyone who can hold a basket is in the rows. The first saffron of the year is carried to the Saffron Palace on a great tray, and the Spice Queen declares the harvest open to trade — the day that sets Al-Khayzar's coin for the year.

festivals.name: The Night of True Names
festivals.description: In Snowend, when the desert nights are longest, the Circle of the Broken Road opens the Archive's star-chamber and the astrologers read the true-name charts beneath the winter constellations. The binding families send their heirs to learn the names they will one day need to command their djinn, and the scholars publicly debate a single point of the Pact's law until dawn — a tradition that is half scholarship and half theater. No djinn is called on this night; the binding families say it is out of respect, the scholars suspect it is because the stars make the calling too potent to risk.

festivals.name: The Great Pearl Dive
festivals.description: In Greenreach, when the reef waters run clearest, the Pearl-Blood Divers hold the Great Dive — the one day the deep reefs are opened to every atoll's divers together, and the season's first and finest pearls are brought up. The Council of Atolls watches from the canoes above, the tattoo-carvers mark each diver's chest with the day's dive-count, and the single largest pearl is offered back to the sea in a ceremony the wayfinders lead at dusk. It is the Archipelago's great day of wealth and pride, and the one day refugees are given equal right to the deep water.

festivals.name: The Rising Tide Memorial
festivals.description: At Thaw, when the year's highest water laps the atoll walls, the islanders walk the perimeter of each atoll at dusk and set floating lamps on the spot where a drowned island once stood. The names of the lost atolls are chanted by the wayfinders from the oldest canoes, the tattoo-carvers display the maps of places that no longer exist, and the refugees of the drowned islands lead the walk on the host atolls. It is the Archipelago's most solemn day — a reckoning with the rising sea that no feast follows, and the day the Council most often argues, afterward, about how many more they can shelter.

_help: What your campaign accumulates. Exactly SEVEN; five of one forges a
Momento — a real item linked to the scenes that earned it.
Leave this out to inherit seven seeded from your genre. If you write your
own, they should be moods a scene can be tagged with, not virtues. Avoid
borrowing another setting's cosmology; that is how a world ends up
wearing someone else's clothes.
`id` is lowercase and stable. `label` is what the panel shows.

set.label: Wonder
set.summary: The feeling of seeing a new place for the first time — a vista, a city, a creature, a sky that is different from the one you were born under.

set.label: Warmth
set.summary: A cozy moment — a shared meal, a bath, a conversation by firelight, the quiet pleasure of being somewhere safe.

set.label: Tension
set.summary: Something is about to break. The air before the argument, the silence before the attack, the pause before a decision that cannot be undone.

set.label: Peril
set.summary: Genuine danger. The ground is not safe. The body is at risk. Something here can hurt you.

set.label: Intrigue
set.summary: Politics, secrets, hidden motives. The sense that what is being said is not what is meant, and that the real conversation is happening somewhere else.

set.label: Sorrow
set.summary: Loss, longing, things that cannot be undone. The weight of what was and is no longer.

set.label: Resolve
set.summary: The moment before a decision. Not the decision itself — the breath before it, when the path is clear and the feet have not yet moved.

_help: Words this world uses for things the engine has generic names for. Keep
it short — this is pinned context and every line costs budget on every
turn. Only include words a narrator would get WRONG without being told.

terms.the currency: trade marks — small stamped metal discs accepted across all seven nations by weight
terms.the ruling body: varies by nation — shogun, king, warlord, jarl, council, or chief depending on where you are
terms.what people call outsiders: farfolk — used everywhere, mildly informal, not insulting
terms.what people call the reincarnated: god-touched — used in most nations; sometimes a compliment, sometimes a warning
terms.what people call the Old Roads: the Old Roads — no other name; everyone knows what you mean

_help: Places. `id` must be unique and is what everything else points at — use
`location:slug` and never change it afterwards.
`parent_location_id` builds the containment tree, and that tree is what
makes jurisdiction real: a patrol belonging to one polity has no business
inside another. Set it even for obvious things.
`map_size_ft` and `rooms` are only needed for interiors you will draw a
floorplan for. Leave them out for a region.
Factions, houses, guilds, companies. `pressure` is the field that makes
one generative rather than decorative: something this group wants that is
not going well, and a sense of how close it is to acting.
NOTE: `pressure` on an organization is stored but nothing moves it yet
(Phase 2, W2.2). Threads already carry a live `pressure`.
People. The player's own character is created with the campaign, not
here — these are everyone else.
`appearance` is prose the image pipeline reads. `visual_identity` is the
anchor that keeps portraits consistent across generations: put the
unchanging things there (hair, eyes, a scar), not today's mood.
`gm_notes` is GM-private and never reaches the narrator or any NPC.
Put what they are hiding there, not in `summary`.
`current_state.location` is LIVE: when the player is at that location,
this person is named to the narrator and the planner as being present.
Use a location id from the block above. `home` is the fallback for
where they are when nothing has moved them.
Bonds between people. Keep the shared and private halves separate:
`public_status` is what anyone can observe; `bond` is your assessment and
stays GM-side.
`disposition` is a number from -100 to 100. It is stored today and does
not drift on its own yet (Phase 2, W2.3).
The engine of the campaign. A thread is something unresolved that will
get worse if ignored.
`next_possible_moves` is the most valuable field in this file. Write the
two or three things that could happen NEXT if the player does nothing.
It is what stops a scene ending on a still frame, and you should revise
it as the campaign moves.
`pressure` here IS live. `stakes` is what is lost if it resolves badly.
Prose. Religions, histories, laws, languages, how the world got here.
Do not reach for a record here unless something must point at it, be
counted, appear in a panel, or be hidden from the player. Until then a
paragraph in your world/*.md files is better — see MIGRATING.md.
`context_tier` controls whether the narrator may reason about it:
pinned (always) / partial (one line) / searchable / hidden.
Objects worth naming. `appearance` feeds the image pipeline; keep story
and provenance in `description`, which the pipeline never reads.
The opening. One campaign is created from this; you can make more later
in the app.
`player_name` and `character_class` are the player's, and the engine
builds their character record. `current_location` must be one of the
location ids above.
campaign.title: The Arrival
campaign.current_quest: Choose which of the seven nations to begin your new life in.
campaign.opening_scene: You wake in a garden you have never seen. The air is warm and still, and the light comes from no direction you can find. Floating islands drift in soft mist around you, and flowers bloom in colors that do not belong to the same season. Ahead, through a grove of trees that are not quite real, stands an open pavilion. A figure is waiting there, seated on the stone bench, watching you with patient dark eyes. Below the pavilion, far below, through layers of cloud, you can see a world spread out — green and gold and blue and white. Seven nations. The figure speaks: 'You have arrived. That is well. I have been waiting. Come, and choose where you will begin.'
